entry.title: So much for taking a break
entry.content:
I have an admission to make: I’m not very good at marketing the stuff I make. I tend to run into my cave, hack for a while, then pop out with something new and yell out “hey look what I made” and when no one notices I shrug and move on.

UMSH feels like it deserves more publicity than I’ve been giving it, so in this post I want to cover what all has happened with UMSH over the past few months and where it is going.

If you’re new here, UMSH is an experimental LoRa mesh protocol for long-range text messaging, similar in spirit to Meshtastic and MeshCore but built with a protocol-first approach (as opposed to a code-first approach). It uses public keys for addresses and has proper cryptography. The firmware and iOS app are open-source software. My last post has the backstory.

In that post I also said I had to stop this breakneck development for at least a month or two. There have been over 600 commits since then, so that didn’t go quite as planned.

There have also been some protocol-breaking changes, so if you ended up trying the firmware or iOS app, you should update your devices and download the iOS app update.

Real-World Deployment

Ben and I have set up 6 repeaters in and around Ashland, Oregon, and we have good coverage there now. Over the next few weeks we hope to expand coverage northward toward Medford and perhaps into Grants Pass and Rogue River. The real-world experience has been invaluable and, so far, things are working quite well.

For example, once we had a few fixed repeaters up, we quickly realized a marginal direct link could actually be worse than no direct link at all.

Sometimes a node might barely hear a distant node before any repeater’s copy of the same packet arrived. It would then decide that the distant node was a direct neighbor, answering it directly. But the distant node might be too far away to hear our node, so the route dies. This can happen even if a repeater right next to our node could have carried the packet without any trouble. Nodes now learn routes from every copy of a reply and score them by signal, so the good path gets a chance to win. Full support for discovering asymmetric routes is coming soon.

Managing those repeaters is easy now, too. You can manage a node over the mesh using the iOS app or using umshctl, without needing to be within Bluetooth range. Text messages now also show which repeaters carried them, and a ping reports the signal at each hop.

Communicator Firmware

In UMSH, we call self-contained devices “communicators”. Getting these up and running has been an important priority over the past few weeks, and we now have a really nice interface running on both the T-LoRa Pager and the T-Deck. Both support all the stuff people have come to expect from chat apps: emojis, reactions, etc. Scrolling is responsive, and the animations slick. And communicators can be used as companion radios, too (although your phone will be its own identity).

You can also run the communicator simulator from the command line: just do a make run-simulator-communicator and it should come up with a fully usable communicator that uses UMSH-over-IP-Multicast for the backend.

Battery life on each of the supported devices is surprisingly good. The T-LoRa Pager has the best battery life, at around a week with GNSS and Wi-Fi turned off. A normal unmodified T-Deck Plus will get decent battery life of 2 days on standby with Wi-Fi and GPS turned off, but if you update the keyboard firmware you can stretch that out to over 4 days!

The keyboard firmware update is something I wrote primarily to address the excessive battery drain of the stock keyboard firmware. The T-Deck’s keyboard is run by its own ESP32-C3, and the stock firmware never let it sleep. This drop-in replacement puts it in a low-power state while the screen is dark, which saves about 13 mA on my T-Deck Plus. Updating the keyboard firmware is not as straightforward as updating the main ESP32-S3 on the device, but once you do you won’t regret it. It is also backward compatible, so if you switch back to Meshtastic or MeshCore the keyboard will still work.

MeshCore Forwarding

UMSH repeaters can now forward MeshCore traffic alongside UMSH traffic. It’s an independent option from UMSH repeating, allowing supported repeaters to forward messages from either protocol, or both! It’s not well tested yet, but if you’d like to give it a shot, let me know how it works out.

To be clear, UMSH and MeshCore users still can’t talk to each other, but one device can now repeat for both—assuming the same LoRa settings.

Everything Else

There is way more that I could go into, but I’ll just leave you with the following:

  • More hardware. In August I said six boards; now the hardware page lists ten, including the T-Beam Supreme and the XIAO ESP32S3 + Wio-SX1262 kit.
  • Internet bridging. Radios in different places can be joined over the internet.
  • UMSH over IP multicast. Nodes on the same network can reach each other with no radio involved.
  • Wi-Fi. Several of the ESP32 boards can join Wi-Fi networks, set up from the app or, on a communicator, from the device itself.
  • Regions. There is now a geographic region database, along with a map for inspecting it. It turns a position into the list of regions a repeater should accept traffic for.
  • The iOS app. Message replies, contact exchange, notifications you can answer from your watch without opening the app, and manual route support.

Where It’s Going

The protocol is still evolving, so expect more breaking changes, even though I hope there will be few going forward. An Android app is planned. Per-sender authentication for group chats is also planned, and now that frames can be signed, a lot of the groundwork is there. The protocol work is all done, it’s just a matter of getting the implementation right.

Ultimately, I’d like to drop the ‘Technology Preview’ label sooner rather than later, and that means building confidence that the underlying protocol is solid. To do that, I need eyeballs and real-world testing.

To be honest, it feels like we are really close! The iOS app and communicator firmware already feel better to me than their Meshtastic/MeshCore counterparts, but perhaps that’s a matter of taste.

If any of this sounds interesting, check out the protocol, join the iOS app beta, flash some hardware, and let me know what you think. You can also just tell someone about it. As I said, I’m not very good at that part.

entry.title: I made a thing...
entry.content:
So… I made a thing. And I’m not sure what to do about it.

I think it’s cool, and I’d like to share it with you, but it’s different than the interactive light sculptures I’ve been making.

First, I made my own secure, off-grid LoRa-based mesh text chat protocol. And then I made a reference implementation for it in Rust. And then I ported that reference implementation to half a dozen different LoRa hardware platforms. And then I wrote an iOS app to control those hardware platforms and send/receive text messages.

I call it UMSH.

Don’t worry, I’m not stopping with the interactive light sculptures—this is a side quest. A bit all-consuming as of late, but still a side quest.

If you are curious how in the world I got to this point, well… read on.

Before I was making interactive light sculptures, I was working at Google on what I described as low-power wireless mesh networking, Thread specifically. I had been doing it for over 10 years. I was tired of it, and needed to do something different that scratched my other creative itches. So I started Voria Labs and started making interactive light sculptures.

But I guess there is still a part of me that really likes doing the low-power wireless mesh networking thing. Several months ago I started looking into LoRa-based mesh text chat protocols, like Meshtastic and MeshCore. These systems allow you to have long-range text communication with groups or individuals that doesn’t rely on cellular infrastructure.

MeshCore, specifically, was interesting to me since the addresses were public keys and it was all source-routed. I started to use it myself, and it was decent enough. Then I went to go look under the hood to see how it was implemented… Well, let’s just say that it was clear that MeshCore took a code-first approach to protocol design.

With a code-first approach, you write the code and get it working, and the source code ends up defining the protocol. This can be OK in certain contexts, but it is often a huge liability. In the case of MeshCore, that liability was a brittle, hard-to-extend protocol with textbook-naive cryptography. A proper fix would practically require compatibility-breaking changes to the protocol.

Which got me to thinking: Knowing what I now know, what would a protocol-first design for something like MeshCore look like? What would a “MeshCore 2.0” be if it was made with a professional-quality protocol-first design with proper cryptography and a flexible packet format?

And that was the start of me falling down the rabbit hole of protocol design again. I love designing protocols. I think I am fairly decent at it. So, on a lark, I started designing what I thought might be a good starting point for a “MeshCore 2.0”.

Now, to be clear, I’m not affiliated with MeshCore in any way. It would be wildly presumptuous of me to actually call whatever-it-was that I was writing “MeshCore 2.0”. But I also can’t really work on something without a name, so I just came up with a random one: UMSH.

I strung together some of my ideas into a semi-coherent document and I brought it up on the MeshCore discord, half expecting to be burned at the stake. Instead, many people seemed fascinated and interested. I kept refining and improving, and eventually what I had was comprehensive protocol documentation.

Even with that, however, there seemed to be little motivation for any serious discussion about a future “MeshCore 2.0”, especially an effort kicked off by an outsider who just came in and said that everything should be done differently. I get it.

At that point, I had a protocol but no implementation. Some time passed. Eventually I decided I should just go for it and see how far me (and Claude) could get with turning the protocol into a working reference implementation. With a full protocol specification in hand, the code would have something to be measured against, instead of becoming the definition itself.

Working with Claude to write code feels a bit like working with an enthusiastic junior software engineer with a short attention span and a habit of micro-dosing LSD. It’s certainly interesting, and I got way more done than I would have otherwise, but I also had to be eagle-eyed about the decisions it was making. It’s certainly not as easy as pointing the LLM at the protocol and saying “implement this”—keeping it on the rails required my full attention and it was a bit exhausting. But it’s hard to argue with the results.

I worked like a madman, thinking “ok, after this feature I’ll stop”, but I kept finding more pain points and more features to implement. After several weeks of work, I now have a quite large chunk of the protocol completely implemented in Rust, as well as a reasonably functional iOS app to go with it. And six supported LoRa hardware platforms. And Wireshark support. And a command-line radio management tool. And a website, with a web-flashing tool.

And now, I must stop this breakneck development for at least a month or two. Maker Faire is coming up, and I just got a really big Lumanoi commission for a project in San Jose that I am extremely excited about.

So now that this is out there, what is next? I’m calling this a technology preview at this stage, so no one mistakes it for something to depend on just yet. I plan to continue to fix bugs and add features based on feedback, and I’m hoping that what I’ve written will resonate with a lot of people. Who knows? Maybe it will take off. Let’s find out.

Check out the protocol, join the iOS app beta, flash some hardware, and let me know what you think.
